description: We are Indonesian students studying across Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, and Australia. Our paths were never meant to cross, yet by chance or destiny, we found each other. We share one belief: what we learn should make the world a better place. Tandborste: Every bristle counts.
summary:
Last Light is a space mission design game built on real NASA data. Set in 2058 at an outpost beside the Apollo 12 landing site, you play an engineer reviving IRIS, an uncrewed science station that went silent four years ago, using Kite, a modular rover you assemble by hand.

Across three missions you follow NASA’s own design loop: set the goal, choose your cargo and rover parts within mass and power limits, check the plan against an energy forecast, then drive it on terrain built from NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter elevation model of the Apollo 12 site. The real slopes and crater shadows decide whether your plan works: the wrong battery runs flat, the wrong wheels get stuck on a loose crater rim, and missing thermal protection freezes Kite in shade. Failure is recoverable, and every mission ends with a report explaining why it succeeded or failed.

Last Light makes the trade-offs behind real space missions something players feel, not just read about.
details:
What it does and how it works

Last Light is a 3D space mission design game set in 2058 at a small outpost next to the Apollo 12 landing site on the Moon. The player is an engineer sent to revive IRIS, an uncrewed science station that went silent four years ago, and to recover the last records of Evan, the engineer who worked there before them. The player never leaves the base to do the science themselves. Instead they plan and run missions with Kite, a modular rover they assemble by hand in the workshop.

Every mission follows the same loop, modelled on how NASA describes the design of a science mission: plan, configure, forecast, drive and report. The player orders cargo on a lander within a mass limit, choosing between a small daytime Courier and a larger Freighter that lands near dusk. They fit Kite with parts such as a 40 Wh or 100 Wh battery, standard or high-grip wheels, a thermal kit and a sampler, each of which changes the rover’s mass and energy use. Before driving out, the mission console forecasts each route’s energy needs against Kite’s range. The player then drives the mission on real lunar terrain, and a Downlink report sends the data home and explains in plain language why the run worked or failed.

The game has three missions. In the first the player assembles Kite and inspects IRIS. In the second they order and retrieve a replacement radio module from a landing zone, restore IRIS and collect a regolith sample. In the third they choose between a short route through Head crater and a longer route around it to reach the far rim, record ground temperatures in sunlight and shade, and bring Evan’s field logger home. If a plan fails, Kite is stranded with its cargo rather than lost: the player can walk out with a limited oxygen supply to carry it back, or call a recovery that costs mission time.

NASA data at the core

The terrain is built from the LROC NAC digital terrain model of the Apollo 12 site from NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, at 2 metre sampling, converted to real metres so slopes are preserved. The real slopes and crater shadows decide which loadouts succeed, so the route choice exists because of the data, not as decoration. Gravity uses NASA’s value of 1.624 m/s², and the cargo landing zone sits away from the outpost because Apollo 12’s descent exhaust sandblasted the nearby Surveyor 3 probe. Elements we simulate, such as the nightfall band and field temperatures, are labelled as simulated in the game, and an in-game Data Sources screen lists every source.

Benefits and intended impact

Mission design is usually taught as a diagram. Last Light lets players learn it through consequences: they make a plan, the Moon tests it, and the report tells them why it worked. Players experience real engineering trade-offs, such as range against mass, traction against energy, and thermal protection against battery life, and they learn the same sequence NASA uses: set goals, design, verify, then fly. It is aimed at secondary and early university students and anyone curious about how space missions are planned, and it is free to play on Windows and macOS. A first full run takes about 20 minutes.

How it is creative

Most space games focus on rockets and orbits. Last Light focuses on surface operations and planning, on terrain that really exists. The player builds the rover with their own hands, checks their design against a forecast, and can see a failure coming before they commit. Failure is treated as information rather than a restart: the stranded rover becomes a rescue problem, and the report turns it into a lesson. The story, an engineer finishing the work a predecessor left behind, gives the engineering decisions an emotional reason to matter.

Tools and technologies

We built the game in the Godot 4.7 engine using GDScript, with 3D models generated through Blender Python scripts. Most of the code, models and sound were produced with AI assistance from Claude (Claude Code), directed, reviewed and playtested by our team. The voices were made with ElevenLabs. Sound effects use Kenney’s CC0 samples and the GeneralUser GS soundfont, and the interface uses the open-licence fonts Michroma, Exo 2 and IBM Plex Mono. We used Git and GitHub with a branch and pull request workflow, ffmpeg to produce the trailer, and more than 60 automated tests, including 12 drive tests that run every loadout down both routes, which we rerun before every merge. No special hardware is needed.

Factors we considered

We wanted the game to be scientifically honest, so measured data and declared game models are kept separate and labelled. We made sure no choice can leave the player stuck: required items are always delivered, and every failure can be recovered from. We balanced the routes so more than one strategy can succeed, and checked that the forecast always shows a failure before the player commits. Playtesting shaped the design: we moved a hard-to-see sample site, reduced on-screen guidance so players could experiment, added the oxygen-limited rescue and made saving visible. We also kept the scope to three focused missions that a cross-border team of four students could finish and polish, checked the licence of every external resource, and listed all of them, including the AI tools, in our references.
